newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian premier takes break as budget battle looms.
newsitem.headline: Russian premier takes break as budget battle looms.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin was starting a three-week holiday on Friday, leaving First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais to tussle with parliament over this year's budget.

Chernomrydin told NTV television in a 15-minute interview devoted to his holiday plans that he would spend his break in his home region of Orenburg in the southern Urals and then in the Black Sea resort of Sochi.
President Boris Yeltsin had approved the leave.
After his return on June 20, Chernomyrdin said he would make official visits to the United States and China.
A government spokeswoman said Chubais, who is also finance minister, would take over cabinet business while Chernomyrdin was away.

The break comes just days before the Duma, Russia's lower house of parliament, reconvenes for a session in which a government budget aimed at tough spending cuts is expected to be the subject of hot debate.
Chubais told a news conference on Friday his main concern was that the Duma might simply block and delay legislation without offering its own solutions for compromise.
Earlier this month, Duma deputies voted by 321 to 11 to delay discussion on the cuts until the government explained how it would raise 30 trillion roubles ($5.2 billion) in extra funds.
The government wants to slash the 1997 budget by one fifth because of a shortfall in tax revenues.
Ministers have made clear that they would ignore any Duma vote against their plans to cut spending. The Duma took months to pass the original 1997 budget bill.

In his interview with NTV, Chernomyrdin said he would spend some of his holiday working on documents and meeting officials. He said he rarely took time off completely from work even before he became prime minister in December 1992. Since then, his vacations had often been interrupted by events, he complained.
The commercial channel intercut the conversation with film comparing the premier's plans to the holiday habits of Soviet leaders from Lenin and Stalin to Mikhail Gorbachev.
It noted that Stalin's vacation planning was dominated by fears of being overthrown, while Nikita Khrushchev and Gorbachev actually did fall victim to coups d'etat while on holiday.
